title: Before erasers, there was bread
hook: For centuries, the way to rub out a pencil mistake was a ball of bread.
peek: Before rubber reached Europe's desks, artists and clerks wiped away pencil marks with pellets of soft bread. In 1770 the scientist Joseph Priestley wrote that a South American gum did the job far better, and the material has been called rubber ever since.
lede: Pencils became common in Europe long before anything existed to correct them. People who made a mistake took a piece of fresh bread, squashed it into a soft ball and dabbed or rubbed the graphite away. In 1770 Joseph Priestley, better known for his work on gases, noted that a gum from South America wiped pencil marks off paper remarkably well.

bullets.text: Priestley described the gum in the preface to a book on drawing in perspective, and said a London instrument maker, Edward Nairne, was selling small cubes of it. Because it rubbed out marks, the material came to be called rubber, a name Priestley is usually credited with.

A popular story says Nairne discovered the trick by accident, grabbing a lump of rubber instead of his usual bread. Nobody can confirm it, but he does seem to have been among the first to sell rubber for erasing.

Raw rubber had a flaw: it turned soft and tacky in summer and hard in winter. Erasers only became reliable after Charles Goodyear's vulcanised rubber in 1839, which stayed firm and springy at any temperature.

Bread never fully disappeared. Some artists still lift charcoal and soft pencil with a pinch of crustless bread, and the modern kneaded eraser does the same job: it is pressed onto the page to pick up graphite rather than scrubbed.
